newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Official dies in make-or-break Albania vote.
newsitem.headline: Official dies in make-or-break Albania vote.

text.p: Voting proceeded briskly on Sunday in an early general election aimed at ending months of unrest in Albania, but sporadic incidents of violence across the Balkan state claimed at least one life.

Both President Sali Berisha, who is trying to retain his Democratic Party's stranglehold on parliament, and his main rival, Socialist leader Fatos Nano, said after casting their votes that they would respect the outcome.

Both men have forecast victory for their parties in a tough campaign, Albania's fourth since the 1990 fall of communism. Both pledge to end the violence in which about 1,500 people have been killed since March.

More than 1,000 candidates from 27 parties are vying for 155 seats -- 115 to be decided in two-round majority races and the rest by a proportional system. The Democrats hold 122 of 140 seats in the outgoing parliament.
The second round will be held next Sunday, pitting the top two candidates against each other in districts where no one wins 50 percent in the first session.
The man shot dead on Sunday was the chief electoral officer in a village near the southern town of Fier. An interior ministry spokesman said a policeman was injured in the melee.
"The crime was politically motivated," the spokesman said by telephone. He said the victim was a member of Berisha's Democrats while the chief suspect had links to the Socialists.
Berisha told reporters in English after voting in a polling station set up in a Tirana school classroom, that he would abide by the outcome of the vote.
"I am definitely going to accept the results. I...will fully recognise the elections," he said.
Berisha, president since 1992, was coy about whether he would stay in office if the Socialists scored a big victory. It was too early, he said, to consider "cohabitation" in Albania.
Nano said the election was the first step of Albania's integration into Europe, seven years after the collapse of one of eastern Europe's most repressive communist regimes.
"These elections are of extraordinary importance," he said. "This will be a society of free citizens no different from other European nations. Tomorrow will be a new day."

The official ATA news agency reported turnout of up to 60 percent by mid-afternoon in many districts, about the same as last year's general election won by Berisha's Democrats but denounced as unfair by international observers.
Queues had formed at most polling stations in Tirana in scorching sunshine.

Polls close at 6 p.m. (1600 GMT), three hours earlier than originally planned, to ensure safety for voters and some 500 international observers ahead of counting. A 7,000-strong International Protection Force dispatched to Albania in April is helping guard polling stations.

Catherine Lalumiere, top official for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe overseeing the vote, said she was pleased with what she saw at Tirana polling stations and spent the afternoon touring other regions by helicopter.
The OSCE has said it is unrealistic for normal Western standards to be attained in Albania's election.
Both main parties have complained of irregularities, mostly voters left off lists. There were also incidents of ballot papers or boxes being stolen or tampered with at gunpoint.

In Mat district, central Albania, no voting was taking place as ballot papers had not been delivered. The OSCE had to reprint papers for 10 districts 48 hours before the vote after election officials complained of errors.
In the south, focal point of months of unrest sparked by the collapse of fraudulent investment schemes, no major incidents were reported.
Predicting the outcome of the vote is virtually impossible.

Berisha was initially lionised by the West for promoting free market policies in the aftermath of communist rule but has been criticised for increasingly authoritarian rule. Many Albanians blame him for the collapse of the investment schemes which left thousands destitute in Europe's poorest country.
The election campaign was conducted under a state of emergency imposed on March 2 to try to quell the unrest. A 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew has been lifted just for election day.
Voters were also asked in a referendum whether they favoured restoring the monarchy. But few believe King Leka I, back from exile, has much chance of returning to the throne.
